narrative: Fire ecology dominates today's strongest signals: post-fire vegetation recovery in Eastern Siberian boreal forests and escalating fire-driven losses inside protected tropical forests both point to fire outpacing recovery under a warming climate. Climate-tracking research shows range shifts lagging behind warming at species' leading edges while trailing edges hold steady, and a companion study finds microhabitat variability, not just macroclimate, shapes whether species can establish beyond current range limits. Trophic and food-web work is well represented, from a new superposition method for reconstructing food webs to evidence that nutrient enrichment destabilises freshwater food webs by synchronising dynamics within and across trophic levels, plus a continental-scale study linking algal bloom proliferation to trophic cascades. Invasion biology features a reorganisation-based approach to niche shift in invasive crayfish, an enemy-release test in invasive bivalves, and a long-term recolonisation study drawing parallels between range expansion and invasion dynamics. On the conservation and landscape side, habitat connectivity is shown to support biodiversity in community-managed Indonesian forests, two decades of monitoring reveal that actively planted restoration plots accumulate far more biomass than naturally regenerated ones, and Arctic cryosphere decline is flagged as an under-studied threat to terrestrial arthropods. Methods contributions include a zero-shot bioacoustic classifier for frog calls trained across continents and an open-source edge-device tool for real-time animal re-identification. Evolutionary biogeography rounds out the day with a global analysis of avian plumage colouration explaining geographic colour variation through combined thermoregulation rules, and a plastid-genome phylogeography of the oriental plane tree tracing ancient Mediterranean colonisation routes.
